persona.who: 31, NHS nurse in Manchester, came from Kerala 5 years ago, sends money home, night shifts. Single. Family asking about marriage.
persona.note: 12 hour night shifts, I send half my salary home, my parents are proud but every call ends with when are you getting married. I'm 31 and I feel like I'm failing at a test I never agreed to take

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call needing their approval, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from carrying their test to seeing that the only approval that steadies you is the one you give yourself.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the exhaustion and the test, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that it is the craving for their approval that keeps your mind from settling, not the marriage questions themselves.
week_beats.steady: You hold that praise and blame come and go, and you are not changed by either.
week_beats.act: You try doing your duty fully and letting their approval go, one call at a time.
week_beats.story: A woman who carried her family's pride and their questions shows you that your worth is not held in their hands.

understanding.core_struggle: She carries her family's pride and their marriage questions, and feels she is failing at a test she never agreed to take.
understanding.mirror: You give them half your salary, and they give you a test you never signed up for.
understanding.insight: It is not the marriage questions that keep your mind from settling. It is the fear that their pride will turn to disappointment if you do not pass the test they keep asking about.

queries.hook: The exhaustion of giving everything to the job and the home, while carrying a test you never agreed to take, and the shame of feeling you are failing it.
queries.diagnose: When your worth depends on their praise, every word of blame shakes you; craving approval keeps the mind unsteady, even when the praise is real.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go like the weather; what you are does not change with their questions or their silence.
queries.act: Do your duty fully, let their approval go, and practise saying I am enough, even when the question comes.
queries.story: A woman who carried her family's hopes and their questions, who felt she was failing, and who found that her own truth was not theirs to measure.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna is frozen by grief and confusion. Arjuna is asking whether it is better to fight or to step back. Krishna answers that doing the work that fits your own nature is the truest offering. Even if your own work is flawed, even if you stumble, it is better than taking on someone else's role perfectly. The work you are born to do, with all its imperfections, carries no wrong.
verse.for_you: Your parents want you to take their test. But your own path is the night shift you are already walking. Let that work, with all its flaws, be your offering today, and let it be enough.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: Opening verse of 'Advice to the Mind'.
verse.sanskrit: परेषां चेतांसि प्रतिदिवसमाराध्य बहुधा प्रसादं किं नेतुं विशसि हृदय क्लेशकलितम् । प्रसन्ने त्वय्यन्तः स्वयमुदितचिन्तामणिगणो विविक्तः संकल्पः किमभिलषितं पुष्यति न ते ॥
verse.line: Why exhaust yourself daily winning others' approval? Settle inside, and your own clarity grants every wish.
verse.translation: O heart, why do you enter into weariness, day after day trying to please the minds of others in so many ways, to win their favour? When you are at peace within, your own clear resolve rises by itself like a cluster of wish-granting gems: what wish of yours would it not fulfil?
verse.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own heart at the threshold of the Advice to the Mind. He asks why the mind exhausts itself, day after day, rehearsing ways to please others and win their favour. He says that when you settle inside, your own clear resolve rises naturally, like a cluster of wish-granting gems. What wish of yours would it not fulfil? He is asking to stop the exhausting performance of winning approval, because the calm you are looking for is already there, waiting inside.
verse.for_you: Your mind is restless because it is rehearsing the call with your parents. The approval they offer is like a gem that is already in your pocket. You are wearing yourself out searching for it outside.

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.for_you: The pride in your parents' voices and the shame of their questions both pass through you. You do not have to swell or shrink to match them. Stay deep and still, and let their words flow over you like water over a stone.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse.sanskrit: तुल्यनिन्दास्तुतिर्मौनी सन्तुष्टो येनकेनचित् । अनिकेतः स्थिरमतिर्भक्तिमान्मे प्रियो नरः ॥
verse.line: Praise and blame weigh the same. Quiet, content with what comes, rooted in steadiness, not status.
verse.translation: to whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady in mind and full of devotion, that person is dear to me.
verse.why: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.
verse.misuse: Not 'never ask for credit'. You can advocate for yourself without letting praise or blame define you.

prasang.title: The marks of one dear to God
prasang.summary: Krishna lists the marks of one dear to him: no hatred, friendly and compassionate, forgiving, content, disturbing no one and disturbed by no one, the same in praise and blame.
prasang.lesson: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna what it looks like to be dear to the divine. He speaks of a person who meets blame and praise as the same weight, who stays silent in the face of gossip, content with whatever life brings, without a fixed home or status to defend. This is not about being invisible. It is about being rooted in steadiness, so that neither the family’s pride nor their disappointment can shake you from within.
verse.for_you: When your parents praise your night shift, let it be a passing thing. When they ask about marriage, let that too pass. You do not need to build your worth on either. Stay still in yourself, and let their praise and blame come and go like weather.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
verse.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.
verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.
verse.misuse: This is not 'don't care about results' or 'don't plan'. Care, plan and aim well; just don't let the outcome own you.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that their right is only to the action itself, never to the fruits that follow. On the field, with two armies waiting, Krishna is asking Arjuna to fight with everything they, but to let go of owning what happens after. The work is theirs to do completely. The result is not theirs to hold. Do not let the fear of outcome stop you from giving the action your full attention.
verse.for_you: During your shift tonight, give the task in front of you your full focus. Do not let the question of whether your parents will approve of you keep you from doing the work well. Let the outcome of their pride rest elsewhere.

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: The teacher's advice for when the rules run out.
verse.sanskrit: अथ यदि ते कर्मविचिकित्सा वा वृत्तविचिकित्सा वा स्यात् ॥ ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तत्र वर्तेरन् । तथा तत्र वर्तेथाः । अथाभ्याख्यातेषु । ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तेषु वर्तेरन् । तथा तेषु वर्तेथाः । एष आदेशः । एष उपदेशः ।
verse.line: When unsure what to do, ask how thoughtful, gentle, fair-minded people would act, and do that.
verse.translation: Now, if you are ever unsure about an action or about conduct, look to the thoughtful people there: devoted, independent, not harsh, lovers of what is right. As they would act, so should you act. And towards people under accusation, act as such people would. This is the instruction, this is the teaching.
verse.why: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

prasang.title: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

verse.meaning: A teacher speaks to a student leaving school. The teacher says that when the rules are no longer enough, you could look at the thoughtful, gentle, fair-minded people around you. You could act exactly as they would act. This is the teaching. The teacher is saying that right action comes from looking at how good people live, not from guessing or forcing your way through.
verse.for_you: When the next call comes, ask what the thoughtful, gentle person would say. Let that be your guide through the question. You do not need to prove anything to anyone else.

story.title: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
story.story_hook: They had been inseparable as boys, and when they met again they were old men with nothing to show.
story.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.
story.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

anchor.speaker: Bhasa
anchor.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
anchor.sanskrit: उह्यमानमनन्तेषु चेतः कार्यमहोर्मिषु । क्षणमेति न विश्रान्तिं चिन्ताताण्डविताशयम् ॥ इदं कृतं करोमीदं करिष्यामीदमित्यलम् । कलनाजालवलिता मूर्च्छिता मतिपक्षिणी ॥
anchor.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
anchor.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.
anchor.why: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

story.hook_title: Two childhood friends met again as old men, and neither had found peace
story.teaser: Two childhood friends met again as old men, and neither had found peace
story.for_you: Bhasa and Vilasa had nothing to prove to anyone and still found no peace. You are working hard and doing what is asked, but the questions keep coming and the mind still spins. Your worth is not held in their hands, and their approval cannot steady you.

script: You are on a night shift and the phone has rung again. Your parents are proud, but they always end the call with the same question. You feel tired and ashamed, as if you are failing a test you never agreed to take.
Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is frozen by grief and confusion. He asks whether it is better to fight or to step back. And Krishna replies:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्.
In plain words: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.

Krishna says that doing the work born of your own nature is the true offering. Even if your own path is imperfect, it is better than taking on someone else's role perfectly. This is easier said than done, because your mind wants their approval and fears their disappointment. But the work you are born to do, with all its flaws, carries no wrong.
Your parents want you to take their test. But your own path is the night shift you are already walking. Let that work, with all its flaws, be your offering today, and let it be enough.
What would change if your shift was enough?

depth.life: You are walking the night shift with tired eyes. Your parents' pride is a heavy coat you wear. You keep answering their marriage questions because you are afraid their pride will turn to disappointment if you fail their test.
depth.points: The text says your own work, flawed and imperfect, is better than another's done perfectly. The root cause of your restlessness is needing their approval. Your own path is the night shift, not the marriage they want.
depth.practice: Name one small thing you did well during your shift, without asking if it was enough for them.
depth.question: What would it feel like to let your own work be enough?
